description: Which CI checks can change their verdict while the tree is unchanged. A 'metadata' rule reads live state outside the committed tree — the pull-request body, the pull-request diff, branch protection, or an external service such as GitHub's dependency-advisory database — so its answer can differ over time or on a body edit or a label change even though no code moved; those rules join the CI-metadata suite and re-run when engine-ci reuses an earlier full-suite proof. A 'code' rule reads only the tree, so a run that has already judged that tree has already judged it. Every rule in the CI suite must appear here exactly once: a self-test fails until a newly added rule is classified, and that self-test independently forces 'metadata' for any rule it can DETECT reaching live state — one handed an API token (pass_token) or one whose target context is the pull-request body, the pull-request diff, or branch protection. Treat that cross-check as a net with known gaps, NOT a proof: a rule that reaches live state some other way — an unauthenticated network read, a token taken from the ambient environment rather than declared via pass_token, or a file CI populates each run — would slip it, and so would a rule reading both a live context and a committed path. So classify honestly by what the rule actually reads; do not assume the net will catch a wrong 'code' answer. A misclassified live-state rule would let a reuse run treat its stale verdict as still valid on a metadata-only event. The question is answered when the rule is written rather than inferred later from a field that cannot fully carry it (a target context is documentary for most rules and, on its own, does not distinguish live state from tree state).
